questions.text: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) SI unit?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the base vs derived units**
The SI system is built on 7 base units (kilogram, metre, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) from which every other unit is derived by combining them through physical definitions.

**Step 2: Test each option**
Newton \( (\text{kg}\, \text{m}\, \text{s}^{-2}) \), Joule \( (\text{kg}\, \text{m}^{2}\, \text{s}^{-2}) \), and Watt \( (\text{kg}\, \text{m}^{2}\, \text{s}^{-3}) \) are all combinations of base units, so they are derived units. Ampere, the unit of electric current, is one of the 7 base units itself.

**Final Answer**
Only a quantity that is not built out of other units qualifies as a base unit.
Final answer: C) Ampere
questions.tip: Memorise the 7 base quantities and units; any unit that can be written as a combination of these (like N, J, W, Pa) is derived, not base.

questions.text: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the base quantity**
Thermodynamic temperature is one of the 7 base quantities of the SI system, and every base quantity has exactly one assigned SI base unit.

**Step 2: Eliminate non-SI scales**
Celsius is a derived, everyday scale related to kelvin by \( T(\text{K}) = T(^{\circ}\text{C}) + 273.15 \); Fahrenheit and Rankine are non-metric scales used outside the SI system entirely.

**Final Answer**
The SI base unit assigned to thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin.
Final answer: C) Kelvin
questions.tip: Kelvin is always used in SI-based formulas (like ideal gas law); Celsius readings must first be converted to kelvin.

questions.text: Which physical quantity has the candela (cd) as its SI unit?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the 7 base quantities and their units**
Among the base quantities, candela is assigned to luminous intensity, the power emitted by a light source in a particular direction weighted by the human eye's sensitivity.

**Step 2: Rule out the derived photometric units**
Luminous flux is measured in lumens (\( \text{cd}\cdot\text{sr} \)), illuminance in lux (\( \text{lm/m}^2 \)), and radiant intensity in watts per steradian -- all derived from candela or from energy units, not base units themselves.

**Final Answer**
Candela is the base unit reserved specifically for luminous intensity.
Final answer: B) Luminous intensity
questions.tip: Candela is the only photometric base unit; flux, illuminance, and intensity-per-area are all derived from it.

questions.text: As per the SI system (post-2019 redefinition), the metre is defined in terms of:
options: Length of a platinum-iridium bar kept at Paris
The distance travelled by light in vacuum in a fixed fraction of a second, using the exact fixed value of the speed of light
The distance between two marks on a standard rod at 0 degree Celsius
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Trace the historical evolution of the metre**
The metre was originally a physical platinum-iridium bar, then redefined via the wavelength of krypton-86 radiation for better reproducibility, since a physical artifact can wear, be damaged, or drift with time.

**Step 2: Apply the modern (post-1983, retained in the 2019 revision) definition**
Today the speed of light in vacuum is fixed by definition at \( c = 299792458 \ \text{m/s} \), and the metre is defined as the distance light travels in vacuum in \( \dfrac{1}{299792458} \) second. This makes the metre reproducible anywhere using atomic clocks and light, without relying on any physical object.

**Final Answer**
Fixing a fundamental constant of nature gives a definition that never drifts, which is why light-based definitions replaced physical artifacts.
Final answer: C) The distance travelled by light in vacuum in a fixed fraction of a second, using the exact fixed value of the speed of light
questions.tip: All 7 SI base units are now defined by fixing exact numerical values of fundamental constants (c, h, e, k_B, N_A, and the Cs-133 transition frequency), not by physical artifacts.

questions.text: The SI unit of amount of substance is the mole. One mole contains a fixed number of elementary entities equal to the Avogadro constant, whose exact defined value is closest to:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the 2019 redefinition of the mole**
Since 2019, the mole is defined by fixing the Avogadro constant exactly as \( N_A = 6.02214076 \times 10^{23} \ \text{mol}^{-1} \), which is approximately \( 6.022 \times 10^{23} \ \text{mol}^{-1} \); one mole is the amount of substance containing exactly this many elementary entities.

**Step 2: Eliminate the constants belonging to other quantities**
\( 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \) is Planck's constant \(h\) (defines the kilogram), \( 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \) is the elementary charge \(e\) (defines the ampere), and \( 9.109 \times 10^{-31} \) kg is simply the electron's rest mass, not a defining SI constant.

**Final Answer**
The mole's definition rests on the fixed Avogadro constant, numerically close to \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\).
Final answer: A) 6.022 x 10^23 per mole
questions.tip: Do not confuse the Avogadro constant (mole), Planck's constant (kilogram), and elementary charge (ampere) -- each fixed constant defines a different base unit.

questions.text: Expressed in terms of SI base units, the unit of pressure (pascal) is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the defining relation**
Pressure is force per unit area, so its SI unit is built by dividing the unit of force by the unit of area.

**Step 2: Substitute base units for force and area**
Force has the base-unit combination \( \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2} \) (from Newton's second law) and area has units \( \text{m}^2 \). Dividing gives
\[ \frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^{2}} = \text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2} \]

**Final Answer**
This combination of base units is exactly what defines one pascal.
Final answer: A) kg m^-1 s^-2
questions.tip: Always derive a unit stepwise from its defining formula (here Pressure = Force/Area) rather than memorising it blindly.

questions.text: In the 2019 redefinition of the SI, the kilogram is now defined by fixing the exact numerical value of:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Understand why the old kilogram artifact was replaced**
The kilogram used to be defined by a physical platinum-iridium cylinder kept in Paris; being a physical object, its mass could drift by micrograms over time, which is unacceptable for a universal standard.

**Step 2: Recall the Kibble balance approach**
A Kibble balance connects mechanical power (involving mass, g, and velocity) to electrical power (involving current and voltage, which trace back to Planck's constant \(h\) via the quantum Hall and Josephson effects) through the relation \( E = h f \). By fixing \( h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \) exactly, mass can be realized from electrical measurements without any physical artifact.

**Final Answer**
The kilogram is now anchored to a fixed value of Planck's constant rather than a physical object.
Final answer: B) Planck's constant h
questions.tip: Remember the pairing: metre <-> speed of light, kilogram <-> Planck's constant, second <-> caesium transition frequency, ampere <-> elementary charge, kelvin <-> Boltzmann constant, mole <-> Avogadro constant.

questions.text: The SI unit of time, the second, is currently defined based on:
options: The period of Earth's revolution around the Sun divided by a fixed number
A defined number of periods of the radiation corresponding to a specific hyperfine transition of the caesium-133 atom
The oscillation period of a quartz crystal oscillator
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recognise the problem with astronomical definitions**
Earlier definitions based on the length of a solar day or the year are not perfectly constant because Earth's rotation and orbital motion have tiny irregularities, making them unsuitable as an unchanging time standard.

**Step 2: Recall the atomic clock definition**
Since 1967, the second has been defined as the duration of exactly \( 9192631770 \) periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the caesium-133 atom, a quantity that is identical everywhere in the universe and does not drift.

**Final Answer**
An atomic transition frequency, not an astronomical motion, defines the modern second.
Final answer: C) A defined number of periods of the radiation corresponding to a specific hyperfine transition of the caesium-133 atom
questions.tip: Atomic clock definitions are preferred because atomic transition frequencies are universal constants, unlike Earth's rotation which slowly changes.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of force is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from Newton's second law**
Force equals mass times acceleration, \( F = ma \), so its dimension is obtained by multiplying the dimension of mass by the dimension of acceleration.

**Step 2: Substitute known dimensions**
Acceleration is velocity per time, i.e. \( [LT^{-1}]/[T] = [LT^{-2}] \). Multiplying by mass \([M]\) gives
\[ [F] = [M][LT^{-2}] = [MLT^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
This is the standard dimensional formula for any force, regardless of its physical origin.
Final answer: A) [MLT^-2]
questions.tip: Build up dimensions from the defining equation rather than memorising a long table -- it transfers to unfamiliar quantities too.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of work (or energy) is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Use the defining formula for work**
Work is force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force, \( W = F \cdot d \).

**Step 2: Multiply the dimensions**
Force has dimension \([MLT^{-2}]\) and displacement has dimension \([L]\), so
\[ [W] = [MLT^{-2}][L] = [ML^{2}T^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
Energy in any form (kinetic, potential, heat) shares this same dimensional formula since they are all interconvertible with work.
Final answer: B) [ML^2T^-2]
questions.tip: Energy and work always share the dimension [ML^2T^-2] -- useful as a quick sanity check for any energy-related formula.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of velocity is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Use the defining formula**
Velocity is displacement covered per unit time, \( v = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}} \).

**Step 2: Substitute base dimensions**
Displacement has dimension \([L]\) and time has dimension \([T]\), so
\[ [v] = \frac{[L]}{[T]} = [LT^{-1}] \]

**Final Answer**
This simple ratio is the building block for deriving the dimensions of acceleration, momentum, force, and energy.
Final answer: A) [LT^-1]
questions.tip: Treat velocity's dimension [LT^-1] as your starting block; acceleration follows by dividing once more by [T].

questions.text: The dimensional formula of pressure is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the defining formula**
Pressure is force acting per unit area, \( P = \dfrac{F}{A} \).

**Step 2: Divide the dimensions**
Force has dimension \([MLT^{-2}]\) and area has dimension \([L^{2}]\), so
\[ [P] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L^{2}]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
This is also the dimensional formula of stress and of the bulk/Young's modulus, since all are force per area.
Final answer: A) [ML^-1T^-2]
questions.tip: Pressure, stress, and elastic moduli (Young's, bulk, shear) all share dimension [ML^-1T^-2] since each is a force divided by an area.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of power is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the defining formula**
Power is the rate at which work is done, \( P = \dfrac{W}{t} \).

**Step 2: Divide dimensions**
Work has dimension \([ML^{2}T^{-2}]\) and time has dimension \([T]\), so
\[ [P] = \frac{[ML^{2}T^{-2}]}{[T]} = [ML^{2}T^{-3}] \]

**Final Answer**
Dividing energy's dimension by one more power of time gives the dimensional formula of power.
Final answer: B) [ML^2T^-3]
questions.tip: Power = Energy/Time, so its dimension is always exactly one power of [T] more negative than energy's.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of angular momentum is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the defining formula**
Angular momentum of a particle is \( L = m v r \), the product of mass, linear velocity, and the perpendicular distance (radius) from the axis.

**Step 2: Multiply the dimensions**
\[ [L] = [M][LT^{-1}][L] = [ML^{2}T^{-1}] \]

**Final Answer**
This dimensional formula also matches Planck's constant, which is why angular momentum quantization (\(L = n\hbar\)) is dimensionally consistent.
Final answer: A) [ML^2T^-1]
questions.tip: Notice angular momentum and Planck's constant share the same dimension [ML^2T^-1] -- a handy cross-check in quantum-mechanics problems.

questions.text: The dimensional formula of surface tension is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the defining formula**
Surface tension is defined as force acting per unit length along the surface, \( T = \dfrac{F}{l} \).

**Step 2: Divide the dimensions**
\[ [T] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L]} = [ML^{0}T^{-2}] = [MT^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
The length dimension cancels out exactly, leaving mass and time only.
Final answer: A) [MT^-2]
questions.tip: Surface tension (force/length) and spring constant (force/displacement) share the identical dimension [MT^-2].

questions.text: Using Newton's law of viscosity, F = eta A (dv/dx), the dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity eta is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Rearrange the defining equation**
From \( F = \eta A \dfrac{dv}{dx} \), the viscosity coefficient is
\[ \eta = \frac{F}{A \left(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\right)} \]

**Step 2: Substitute dimensions of each factor**
\([F] = [MLT^{-2}]\), \([A] = [L^{2}]\), and the velocity gradient \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\) has dimension \(\dfrac{[LT^{-1}]}{[L]} = [T^{-1}]\).

**Step 3: Combine**
\[ [\eta] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L^{2}][T^{-1}]} = [MLT^{-2}] \cdot [L^{-2}] \cdot [T] = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}] \]

**Final Answer**
Breaking a compound formula into individual factor dimensions before combining avoids sign errors in the exponents.
Final answer: A) [ML^-1T^-1]
questions.tip: When a formula has a derivative term like dv/dx, treat it dimensionally as an ordinary ratio of the two dimensions involved.

questions.text: Using the relation E = h f (Planck's relation, where f is frequency), the dimensional formula of Planck's constant h is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Rearrange Planck's relation**
From \( E = hf \), we get \( h = \dfrac{E}{f} \).

**Step 2: Substitute known dimensions**
Energy has dimension \([ML^{2}T^{-2}]\) and frequency (cycles per second) has dimension \([T^{-1}]\), so
\[ [h] = \frac{[ML^{2}T^{-2}]}{[T^{-1}]} = [ML^{2}T^{-1}] \]

**Final Answer**
This matches the dimension of angular momentum, confirming h and angular momentum are dimensionally the same kind of quantity (action).
Final answer: A) [ML^2T^-1]
questions.tip: Quantities with dimension [ML^2T^-1] are called 'action' -- Planck's constant and angular momentum both belong to this family.

questions.text: Using Newton's law of gravitation, F = G m1 m2 / r^2, the dimensional formula of the gravitational constant G is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Rearrange the gravitation formula**
From \( F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2} \), we isolate G:
\[ G = \frac{Fr^{2}}{m_1m_2} \]

**Step 2: Substitute dimensions**
\([F] = [MLT^{-2}]\), \([r^2] = [L^2]\), and the product \(m_1m_2\) has dimension \([M^2]\), so
\[ [G] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}][L^{2}]}{[M^{2}]} = [M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
The negative power of mass arises because G divides out one full factor of \([M^2]\) while only one \([M]\) is supplied by force.
Final answer: A) [M^-1L^3T^-2]
questions.tip: For any 'constant of proportionality' in a physical law, isolate it algebraically first, then substitute dimensions of every other quantity.

questions.text: The principle of homogeneity of dimensions states that:
options: All terms that are added, subtracted, or equated in a physical equation must have the same dimensions
All physical quantities must be measured in SI units
Every equation must contain at least three fundamental quantities
Dimensionless quantities can never appear in a valid equation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Understand what the principle actually claims**
The principle of homogeneity is about consistency of dimensions across an equation, not about which unit system is used or how many fundamental quantities appear.

**Step 2: Eliminate the incorrect statements**
An equation can be dimensionally correct in any consistent unit system (CGS, FPS, or SI), so option B is false. There is no requirement of exactly three quantities (option C), and dimensionless terms (like angles or trigonometric arguments) frequently and validly appear in physical equations, so option D is also false.

**Final Answer**
Only terms that are added, subtracted, or set equal to each other must share identical dimensions -- that is the actual content of the principle.
Final answer: A) All terms that are added, subtracted, or equated in a physical equation must have the same dimensions
questions.tip: Use this principle first to check any unfamiliar formula: mismatched dimensions between added terms instantly signal an error.

questions.text: Which of the following expressions is dimensionally consistent for the time period T of a simple pendulum of length l in a gravitational field g?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compute the dimension needed**
Time period T must have dimension \([T]\); the numerical factor \(2\pi\) is dimensionless and does not affect this check.

**Step 2: Test option A**
\( l \) has dimension \([L]\) and \(g\) has dimension \([LT^{-2}]\), so
\[ \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{[L]}{[LT^{-2}]}} = \sqrt{[T^{2}]} = [T] \]
This matches the required dimension of T.

**Step 3: Rule out the others**
\(\sqrt{g/l}\) gives \([T^{-1}]\) (a frequency, not a time), \(\sqrt{lg}\) gives \([L T^{-1}]\) (a velocity), and \(l/g\) gives \([T^{2}]\) -- none match \([T]\).

**Final Answer**
Only the square root of (length/g) yields the correct time dimension.
Final answer: A) T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g)
questions.tip: When choosing between similar-looking formulas, plug in dimensions rather than trying to recall the formula from memory.

questions.text: In mechanics, the dimensional formula of any derived physical quantity is expressed in terms of how many fundamental (base) quantities?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the base quantities relevant to mechanics**
While the full SI system recognises 7 base quantities overall, purely mechanical quantities (like force, energy, pressure, momentum) are built only from mass, length, and time.

**Step 2: Confirm with examples**
Force is \([MLT^{-2}]\), energy is \([ML^{2}T^{-2}]\), and pressure is \([ML^{-1}T^{-2}]\) -- every mechanical quantity's dimensional formula uses only M, L, and T, never current, temperature, luminous intensity, or amount of substance.

**Final Answer**
Mechanical quantities always reduce to combinations of exactly three base dimensions.
Final answer: B) 3
questions.tip: Electrical, thermal, and photometric quantities bring in the extra base dimensions (A, K, cd, mol); pure mechanics never needs more than M, L, T.

questions.text: Using dimensional analysis, the time period T of a simple pendulum is assumed to depend on its length l, the mass m of the bob, and the acceleration due to gravity g, as T = k l^a m^b g^c. Dimensional analysis shows that:
options: T is proportional to sqrt(l/g) and is independent of m
T is proportional to m sqrt(l/g)
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the dimensional equation**
Writing \( T = k\, l^{a} m^{b} g^{c} \) and substituting dimensions on both sides:
\[ [T] = [L]^{a}[M]^{b}[LT^{-2}]^{c} = [M]^{b}[L]^{a+c}[T]^{-2c} \]

**Step 2: Equate powers of M, L, T separately**
Comparing exponents: for M, \(b = 0\); for T, \(-2c = 1 \Rightarrow c = -\dfrac{1}{2}\); for L, \(a + c = 0 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

**Step 3: Substitute back**
With \(a = 1/2,\ b = 0,\ c = -1/2\), we get \( T = k\, l^{1/2} m^{0} g^{-1/2} = k\sqrt{l/g} \), showing T does not depend on the mass of the bob at all.

**Final Answer**
This is exactly why a pendulum's period is independent of the mass of its bob -- a result dimensional analysis predicts before any experiment.
Final answer: A) T is proportional to sqrt(l/g) and is independent of m
questions.tip: With three base dimensions (M, L, T) you get exactly three equations, letting you solve for up to three unknown exponents uniquely.

questions.text: The terminal velocity v of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid depends on its radius r, the density difference between sphere and fluid (delta rho), the viscosity eta of the fluid, and acceleration due to gravity g. Dimensional analysis gives v proportional to:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the physical combination to test**
Stokes' law for terminal velocity is \( v = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^{2}(\Delta\rho) g}{\eta} \); we verify this combination is dimensionally a velocity.

**Step 2: Write the dimensions of each factor**
\([r^2] = [L^2]\), \([\Delta\rho] = [ML^{-3}]\), \([g] = [LT^{-2}]\), and \([\eta] = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}]\).

**Step 3: Combine numerator and divide by eta**
Numerator: \([L^2][ML^{-3}][LT^{-2}] = [M L^{0} T^{-2}]\). Dividing by \([\eta] = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}]\):
\[ \frac{[ML^{0}T^{-2}]}{[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]} = [L^{1}T^{-1}] \]
which is exactly the dimension of velocity, \([LT^{-1}]\).

**Final Answer**
Only the combination \( r^2 (\Delta\rho) g/\eta \) reduces correctly to a velocity dimension.
Final answer: A) r^2 (delta rho) g / eta
questions.tip: For a multi-variable dependence, check the final combined dimension against the target quantity's dimension rather than solving all exponents from scratch when the formula is already known.

questions.text: A student writes the displacement in simple harmonic motion as x = A sin(omega t + phi). For this equation to be dimensionally valid, the argument (omega t + phi) of the sine function must be:
options: Have the same dimension as x
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall why this restriction exists**
Trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions are defined through infinite power series (e.g. \( \sin\theta = \theta - \theta^3/3! + \dots \)); adding terms like \(\theta\) and \(\theta^3\) is only dimensionally valid if \(\theta\) itself is a pure number.

**Step 2: Verify with the given quantities**
Angular frequency \(\omega\) has dimension \([T^{-1}]\) and time t has dimension \([T]\), so their product \(\omega t\) is dimensionless. The phase constant \(\phi\) must also be dimensionless (measured in radians) so it can be validly added to \(\omega t\).

**Final Answer**
Any quantity appearing as the argument of sin, cos, exp, or log must be dimensionless, regardless of the physical context.
Final answer: A) Dimensionless
questions.tip: Whenever you see sin, cos, exp, or log in a formula, immediately check that whatever sits inside is dimensionless -- this is a very common JEE/NEET trap.

questions.text: Given the equation of motion v = u + at, dimensional analysis shows that this equation is:
options: Dimensionally correct, since v, u, and at all have dimension [LT^-1]
Dimensionally incorrect, since a and t cannot be added
Dimensionally correct only when a is constant
Dimensionally incorrect, since v and u have different dimensions
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the dimension of every term**
\(v\) and \(u\) are both velocities, so \([v] = [u] = [LT^{-1}]\). Acceleration \(a\) has dimension \([LT^{-2}]\) and time \(t\) has dimension \([T]\).

**Step 2: Check the product term**
\[ [at] = [LT^{-2}][T] = [LT^{-1}] \]
which matches the dimension of v and u exactly.

**Step 3: Apply the principle of homogeneity**
Since all three terms being added/equated (v, u, and at) share the identical dimension \([LT^{-1}]\), the equation is dimensionally consistent, though this check alone cannot confirm the numerical coefficient is correct -- only that the structure is valid.

**Final Answer**
All terms match in dimension, so the kinematic equation passes the homogeneity test.
Final answer: A) Dimensionally correct, since v, u, and at all have dimension [LT^-1]
questions.tip: Dimensional correctness is necessary but not sufficient for an equation to be physically true -- it only rules out dimensionally inconsistent equations.

questions.text: Dimensional analysis fails to give the complete, exact form of a physical equation when:
options: The equation involves a dimensionless numerical constant (such as 1/2 or 4 pi^2) that cannot be fixed by matching dimensions alone
The physical quantity involved has more than one type of dimension
SI units are not used consistently throughout the calculation
The equation involves exactly three fundamental quantities
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Understand what dimensional analysis can and cannot fix**
Dimensional analysis can determine how a quantity depends on the powers of other quantities, since matching dimensions gives equations for those exponents; but a pure number, like the \(1/2\) in \(KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) or the \(4\pi^2\) in the pendulum formula, has no dimension at all.

**Step 2: See why this makes the constant unreachable**
Since a dimensionless constant carries dimension \([M^0L^0T^0]\), it never enters or affects the dimensional matching equations -- there is simply no dimensional equation left to solve for it, so it must instead be found by experiment or by full derivation.

**Final Answer**
This is the classic and genuine limitation of the dimensional method: dimensionless multiplying constants remain undetermined.
Final answer: A) The equation involves a dimensionless numerical constant (such as 1/2 or 4 pi^2) that cannot be fixed by matching dimensions alone
questions.tip: Always remember: dimensional analysis gives you the form of a relation up to an unknown dimensionless constant, never the constant's numerical value.

questions.text: Which of the following is a genuine limitation of the method of dimensional analysis?
options: It cannot be used to check whether an equation is dimensionally correct

It cannot uniquely derive a relation depending on more than three independent quantities when only mass, length, and time are involved, since only three equations are available to solve for the exponents
It cannot ever be applied to equations involving trigonometric functions
It works only for mechanical quantities and never applies to any other branch of physics
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how many independent equations dimensional matching provides**
In mechanics, comparing dimensions gives exactly three simultaneous equations, one each for the powers of M, L, and T.

**Step 2: See what happens with more than three unknowns**
If a quantity is assumed to depend on four or more independent quantities (four unknown exponents), the three available equations are not enough to solve for all of them uniquely -- this is the real limitation.

**Step 3: Eliminate the false statements**
Option A is false, since checking dimensional correctness is exactly what the method does well. Option C is false because trigonometric functions can appear as long as their argument is dimensionless. Option D is false since dimensional analysis is used across electricity, thermodynamics, and other branches too, using the extra base dimensions A, K, mol, cd as needed.

**Final Answer**
The true limitation is the mismatch between the number of unknown exponents and the fixed number of dimensional equations available.
Final answer: B) It cannot uniquely derive a relation depending on more than three independent quantities when only mass, length, and time are involved, since only three equations are available to solve for the exponents
questions.tip: Count the number of independent variables in a proposed relation; if it exceeds the number of base dimensions being used, dimensional analysis alone cannot solve it uniquely.

questions.text: In the van der Waals equation (P + a/V^2)(V - b) = RT, where P is pressure and V is volume, the dimensional formula of the constant a is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the principle of homogeneity**
Inside the bracket \((P + a/V^2)\), the term \(a/V^2\) is being added to pressure P, so by the principle of homogeneity it must have exactly the same dimension as pressure.

**Step 2: Set up the dimensional equation**
\[ [a] = [P][V^{2}] \]
where \([P] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]\) and \([V] = [L^{3}]\), so \([V^2] = [L^{6}]\).

**Step 3: Combine**
\[ [a] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L^{6}] = [ML^{5}T^{-2}] \]

**Final Answer**
The principle of homogeneity lets us find the dimension of an unknown constant just by matching it against the term it is added to.
Final answer: A) [ML^5T^-2]
questions.tip: Whenever a constant is added to a known physical quantity inside brackets, its dimension must equal that quantity's dimension -- use this shortcut to find dimensions of unfamiliar constants.

questions.text: The absolute error in a single measurement is defined as:
options: The magnitude of the difference between the true (or mean) value and the measured value
The ratio of the error to the true value
The percentage deviation of the measured value from the mean
The smallest division on the measuring instrument
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the definition**
Absolute error for a single reading \(a_i\) is defined as \( \Delta a_i = |a_{\text{true}} - a_i| \); when the true value is unknown, the mean of many readings \(a_{\text{mean}}\) is used as the best estimate in its place.

**Step 2: Distinguish from related terms**
The ratio to the true value (option B) is relative error, its percentage form (option C) is percentage error, and the smallest division of an instrument (option D) is its least count -- a separate concept describing instrument resolution, not the actual deviation of a reading.

**Final Answer**
Absolute error is simply the magnitude of the deviation of a single reading from the best (true or mean) value.
Final answer: A) The magnitude of the difference between the true (or mean) value and the measured value
questions.tip: Keep the chain clear: absolute error (has units) -> relative error (unitless ratio) -> percentage error (relative error x 100).

questions.text: Systematic errors in an experiment arise due to:
options: Random and unpredictable fluctuations by the observer
Known, reproducible causes such as instrument zero error, imperfect design, or faulty calibration, and they tend to occur in a definite direction
Unknown causes that can never be identified or corrected
Errors that always average out to zero over many readings
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the source of systematic error**
Systematic errors come from identifiable, reproducible causes: instrumental defects (a mis-calibrated scale, zero error), imperfect experimental technique, or a consistent personal bias of the observer.

**Step 2: Note the key distinguishing feature**
Because the cause is fixed and reproducible, systematic errors push every reading in the same direction (always too high or always too low), unlike random errors, which fluctuate irregularly in both directions and partly cancel out when averaged over many trials.

**Final Answer**
Since the cause is known and one-directional, systematic errors can usually be estimated and corrected once identified -- this is what distinguishes them from random errors.
Final answer: B) Known, reproducible causes such as instrument zero error, imperfect design, or faulty calibration, and they tend to occur in a definite direction
questions.tip: Random errors are reduced by taking the mean of many readings; systematic errors are reduced by correcting or recalibrating the instrument or method, since averaging does not remove them.

questions.text: The least count of a vernier caliper is given by:
options: Value of one main scale division minus value of one vernier scale division
Value of one main scale division plus value of one vernier scale division
Number of vernier divisions divided by one main scale division
Total length of the vernier scale divided by the main scale division
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how the vernier scale is constructed**
A vernier scale is built so that n vernier scale divisions (VSD) exactly span (n-1) main scale divisions (MSD); this deliberate mismatch is what allows fine reading between main scale marks.

**Step 2: Derive the least count from this mismatch**
The least count is the smallest length this mismatch can resolve, which works out to
\[ \text{Least count} = 1\ \text{MSD} - 1\ \text{VSD} \]
representing the tiny difference between one main scale division and one vernier scale division.

**Final Answer**
This difference, not a sum or a simple division, is what defines the instrument's least count.
Final answer: A) Value of one main scale division minus value of one vernier scale division
questions.tip: For a standard vernier caliper (1 MSD = 1 mm, 10 VSD = 9 MSD), this gives the familiar least count of 0.1 mm -- rederive it rather than memorising only the final number.

questions.text: The length of a rod is measured five times as 25.2 cm, 25.3 cm, 25.1 cm, 25.4 cm, and 25.2 cm. The mean absolute error in the measurement is closest to:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compute the mean value**
\[ a_{\text{mean}} = \frac{25.2+25.3+25.1+25.4+25.2}{5} = \frac{126.2}{5} = 25.24\ \text{cm} \]

**Step 2: Compute the absolute deviation of each reading**
\( |25.2-25.24| = 0.04 \), \( |25.3-25.24| = 0.06 \), \( |25.1-25.24| = 0.14 \), \( |25.4-25.24| = 0.16 \), \( |25.2-25.24| = 0.04 \).

**Step 3: Average the absolute deviations**
\[ \Delta a_{\text{mean}} = \frac{0.04+0.06+0.14+0.16+0.04}{5} = \frac{0.44}{5} = 0.088 \approx 0.09\ \text{cm} \]

**Final Answer**
The reported result would therefore be written as \( (25.24 \pm 0.09)\ \text{cm} \).
Final answer: A) 0.09 cm
questions.tip: Always compute the mean first, then find each deviation from that mean, not from any single reading.

questions.text: The length and breadth of a rectangular plate are measured as l = (5.0 +/- 0.1) cm and b = (3.0 +/- 0.1) cm. The absolute error in the perimeter P = 2(l+b) is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the rule for addition/subtraction of errors**
When quantities are added or subtracted, their absolute errors simply add together, since in the worst case both individual errors could act in the same direction.

**Step 2: Apply it to l + b**
\[ \Delta(l+b) = \Delta l + \Delta b = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2\ \text{cm} \]

**Step 3: Scale by the constant multiplier**
Since \(P = 2(l+b)\) and multiplying by an exact constant scales the absolute error by that same constant,
\[ \Delta P = 2 \times \Delta(l+b) = 2 \times 0.2 = 0.4\ \text{cm} \]

**Final Answer**
The perimeter should be reported as \( P = (16.0 \pm 0.4)\ \text{cm} \).
Final answer: A) 0.4 cm
questions.tip: Absolute errors add for sums and differences; do not divide or average them -- always take the worst-case sum.

questions.text: A resistance is determined using R = V/I, where V = (20.0 +/- 0.2) V and I = (4.0 +/- 0.1) A. The percentage error in R is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the rule for multiplication/division of errors**
When quantities are multiplied or divided, their relative (fractional) errors add together, regardless of whether the operation is multiplication or division.

**Step 2: Compute each relative error**
\[ \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{0.2}{20.0} = 0.01, \qquad \frac{\Delta I}{I} = \frac{0.1}{4.0} = 0.025 \]

**Step 3: Add and convert to percentage**
\[ \frac{\Delta R}{R} = \frac{\Delta V}{V} + \frac{\Delta I}{I} = 0.01 + 0.025 = 0.035 = 3.5\% \]

**Final Answer**
The measured resistance carries an uncertainty of about 3.5% due to combining the errors in V and I.
Final answer: A) 3.5%
questions.tip: For products and quotients, always add relative (percentage) errors, never absolute errors directly.

questions.text: The density of a cube is calculated using rho = m/V, where V = (side)^3. If the mass is measured with 2% error and each side of the cube is measured with 1% error, the percentage error in the calculated density is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the power rule to find the error in volume**
Since \(V = (\text{side})^3\), the power rule says the relative error in volume is 3 times the relative error in a single side:
\[ \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \times \frac{\Delta(\text{side})}{\text{side}} = 3 \times 1\% = 3\% \]

**Step 2: Combine mass and volume errors using the division rule**
Since \(\rho = m/V\), the relative errors of m and V add:
\[ \frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 2\% + 3\% = 5\% \]

**Final Answer**
The cubic dependence on side length amplifies its error threefold before it even combines with the mass error.
Final answer: A) 5%
questions.tip: Whenever a quantity is raised to a power n in a formula, its contribution to the percentage error gets multiplied by n -- this is the single most tested error-propagation rule.

questions.text: A screw gauge has 50 divisions on its circular scale and a pitch of 1 mm. Its least count is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of pitch and least count**
The pitch is the linear distance the screw advances in one complete rotation of the circular scale, and the least count is the smallest length the instrument can resolve, found by dividing the pitch by the number of divisions on the circular scale.

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
\[ \text{Least count} = \frac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of circular scale divisions}} = \frac{1\ \text{mm}}{50} = 0.02\ \text{mm} \]

**Final Answer**
A finer division count on the circular scale directly gives a smaller (better) least count for the same pitch.
Final answer: A) 0.02 mm
questions.tip: Least count of a screw gauge = Pitch / (number of circular scale divisions); do not confuse pitch with least count itself.

questions.text: When reporting the result of a series of measurements with mean value a_mean and mean absolute error Delta a_mean, the correct way to express the result is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the purpose of reporting an error**
A measurement result should communicate both the best estimate of the quantity and the range within which the true value is expected to lie.

**Step 2: Apply the standard convention**
By convention, the result is written as \( a = a_{\text{mean}} \pm \Delta a_{\text{mean}} \), indicating the true value most likely lies between \( a_{\text{mean}} - \Delta a_{\text{mean}} \) and \( a_{\text{mean}} + \Delta a_{\text{mean}} \).

**Final Answer**
This plus-minus notation is the universal way physical measurements are reported alongside their uncertainty.
Final answer: A) a = a_mean +/- Delta a_mean
questions.tip: Always report both the central value and its uncertainty together -- a number without its error estimate is scientifically incomplete.

questions.text: In determining g using a simple pendulum via g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2, the length L is measured with 1% error and the time period T (from many oscillations) has 2% error. The percentage error in the calculated value of g is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the powers involved**
In \( g = 4\pi^2 L T^{-2} \), L appears to the first power and T appears to the power -2 (the numerical factor \(4\pi^2\) is exact and contributes no error).

**Step 2: Apply the power rule for each factor**
\[ \frac{\Delta g}{g} = 1 \times \frac{\Delta L}{L} + 2 \times \frac{\Delta T}{T} = 1\% + 2(2\%) = 1\% + 4\% = 5\% \]

**Final Answer**
Because T is squared in the denominator, its error contributes twice as much as L's error, making timing precision the dominant factor in this experiment.
Final answer: A) 5%
questions.tip: In compound formulas, multiply each variable's relative error by the magnitude of its power before summing -- squared or cubed terms dominate the total error.

questions.text: A metre scale has a positive zero error of 0.2 cm (it reads 0.2 cm even when the object length is actually zero). If the raw scale reading for a table's length is 150.5 cm, the corrected (true) length is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Understand what a positive zero error means**
A positive zero error means the instrument's scale is systematically shifted so that it reads a value higher than the true reading at every point, including at zero.

**Step 2: Apply the correction rule**
Since every raw reading includes this extra 0.2 cm baked in, the correction rule is:
\[ \text{True reading} = \text{Observed reading} - (\text{positive zero error}) \]

**Step 3: Substitute the given values**
\[ \text{True length} = 150.5 - 0.2 = 150.3\ \text{cm} \]

**Final Answer**
Subtracting the known, reproducible zero error removes this systematic bias from the raw reading.
Final answer: A) 150.3 cm
questions.tip: Remember the sign convention: subtract a positive zero error, add (i.e. subtract a negative number) a negative zero error, to get the corrected reading.

questions.text: The kinetic energy of a particle is E = (1/2) m v^2. If the velocity v is measured with a 3% error and the mass is measured with negligible error, the percentage error in the calculated kinetic energy is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the power of each error-carrying variable**
In \( E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \), mass contributes negligible error, but velocity appears raised to the power 2; the constant \(1/2\) contributes no error since it is an exact number.

**Step 2: Apply the power rule**
By the power rule, the relative error in v^2 is twice the relative error in v:
\[ \frac{\Delta E}{E} = 2 \times \frac{\Delta v}{v} = 2 \times 3\% = 6\% \]

**Final Answer**
Squaring a variable in a formula doubles its fractional contribution to the final error, so a small 3% velocity error becomes a 6% energy error.
Final answer: A) 6%
questions.tip: In kinetic energy problems, always remember velocity's error gets doubled because of the square -- this small detail is a frequent scoring point in JEE/NEET.

questions.text: The number of significant figures in the measurement 0.006050 is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the rule for leading zeros**
Zeros appearing before the first non-zero digit (here, the zeros in 0.00) are never significant -- they only fix the position of the decimal point.

**Step 2: Apply the rule for digits after the first non-zero digit**
Starting from the first non-zero digit, every digit counts as significant, including any zeros that follow, since the number is written with a decimal point: the digits are 6, 0, 5, 0.

**Final Answer**
Counting these four digits gives the total number of significant figures.
Final answer: A) 4
questions.tip: Leading zeros are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are always significant.

questions.text: According to the rules of significant figures, trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point (for example, 4500) are:
options: Ambiguous -- they may or may not be significant, so scientific notation is used to remove the ambiguity
Significant only if the quantity is a measured length
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recognise the ambiguity**
Written as 4500, it is unclear whether the trailing zeros are placeholders (giving only 2 significant figures) or were actually measured precisely (giving up to 4 significant figures).

**Step 2: Recall how this ambiguity is resolved**
Scientific notation removes the ambiguity entirely: \( 4.5 \times 10^{3} \) unambiguously has 2 significant figures, while \( 4.500 \times 10^{3} \) unambiguously has 4 significant figures.

**Final Answer**
Trailing zeros without a decimal point are inherently ambiguous, which is precisely why scientific notation is the preferred way to report such measurements.
Final answer: A) Ambiguous -- they may or may not be significant, so scientific notation is used to remove the ambiguity
questions.tip: Whenever trailing zeros in a whole number look ambiguous, rewrite the number in scientific notation to make the significant figure count explicit.

questions.text: In the measurement 3.0500 x 10^4 m, the number of significant figures is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the rule for scientific notation**
In scientific notation, every digit written in the coefficient (the part before x 10^power) is significant; the power of ten itself never adds or removes significant figures.

**Step 2: Count the digits in the coefficient**
The coefficient is 3.0500, containing the digits 3, 0, 5, 0, 0 -- all five are significant because they lie between and after non-zero digits, following a decimal point.

**Final Answer**
Scientific notation makes the count unambiguous: five significant figures.
Final answer: A) 5
questions.tip: In scientific notation, simply count every digit shown in the coefficient -- the exponent never affects the significant figure count.

questions.text: Add the following measured lengths applying the correct significant figure rule: 12.11 cm + 18.0 cm + 1.012 cm. The properly rounded result is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the addition/subtraction rule**
For addition or subtraction, the result must be rounded to the same number of decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places, since that term is the least precisely known.

**Step 2: Identify the limiting term**
Among 12.11 (2 decimal places), 18.0 (1 decimal place), and 1.012 (3 decimal places), the term 18.0 has the fewest decimal places (only 1), so it limits the precision of the final answer.

**Step 3: Add and round**
Raw sum: \( 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 = 31.122 \). Rounding to 1 decimal place (matching 18.0) gives 31.1 cm.

**Final Answer**
The least precisely known term always sets the number of decimal places retained in a sum.
Final answer: A) 31.1 cm
questions.tip: For addition/subtraction, match decimal places (not the total count of significant figures) to the least precise term.

questions.text: Multiply 4.237 (4 significant figures) by 2.1 (2 significant figures). The properly rounded product is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the multiplication/division rule**
For multiplication or division, the final result must be rounded to the same number of significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures.

**Step 2: Identify the limiting factor**
4.237 has 4 significant figures, while 2.1 has only 2 significant figures, so the answer must be reported to 2 significant figures.

**Step 3: Multiply and round**
Raw product: \( 4.237 \times 2.1 = 8.8977 \). Rounded to 2 significant figures, this becomes 8.9.

**Final Answer**
The factor with fewer significant figures (2.1) controls the precision of the final product.
Final answer: A) 8.9
questions.tip: For multiplication/division, match the total count of significant figures (not decimal places) to the least precise factor.

questions.text: Round off 6.3752 to 3 significant figures.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the digits to be retained**
Rounding to 3 significant figures means keeping the digits 6, 3, and 7, and deciding how the next digit affects the last retained digit.

**Step 2: Examine the digit after the cutoff**
The digit immediately after 7 is 5, and it is followed by further non-zero digits (2), so the discarded part (0.052...) is greater than half a unit in the last retained place.

**Step 3: Round accordingly**
Since the discarded portion exceeds half, the last retained digit is rounded up: 7 becomes 8, giving 6.38.

**Final Answer**
Because more than just an exact 5 remains, the ordinary round-up rule applies here.
Final answer: A) 6.38
questions.tip: Look beyond just the very next digit when deciding how to round -- any non-zero digits further along confirm a clear round-up.

questions.text: A measured value is written as 2.30 x 10^3 m. The number of significant figures in this value is:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall why scientific notation is used here**
Writing the value as 2300 m alone would leave the trailing zeros ambiguous, but scientific notation removes that ambiguity by showing exactly which digits were measured.

**Step 2: Count the digits in the coefficient**
The coefficient 2.30 contains the digits 2, 3, and 0, and since the zero appears after the decimal point in the coefficient, it is deliberately significant, confirming the measurement was precise to that digit.

**Final Answer**
All three digits shown in the coefficient are significant.
Final answer: A) 3
questions.tip: Writing a trailing zero explicitly in the coefficient of scientific notation is a deliberate statement that it was measured, not just a placeholder.

questions.text: The perimeter of a rectangle with length l = 5.7 cm and breadth b = 3.42 cm is computed as P = 2(l + b). Using correct significant figure rules, P should be reported as:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the addition rule to l + b first**
For addition, the result is limited by the term with the fewest decimal places; here 5.7 has only 1 decimal place while 3.42 has 2, so the sum must be rounded to 1 decimal place.
\[ 5.7 + 3.42 = 9.12 \rightarrow \text{rounded to } 9.1\ \text{cm} \]

**Step 2: Multiply by the exact factor of 2**
The factor 2 in \(P = 2(l+b)\) is an exact counting number (not a measured quantity), so it does not limit the significant figures further:
\[ P = 2 \times 9.1 = 18.2\ \text{cm} \]

**Final Answer**
Because the intermediate addition is rounded first, the final perimeter correctly reflects the precision of the least precise length measurement.
Final answer: A) 18.2 cm
questions.tip: Exact numbers (counting factors like the '2' in a perimeter formula) are treated as having infinite significant figures and never limit the final precision.

questions.text: Round 2.745 to 3 significant figures using the round-half-to-even convention (used to avoid a systematic bias when the digit to be dropped is exactly 5 with nothing beyond it).
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the round-half-to-even rule**
When the digit being dropped is exactly 5 with no further non-zero digits after it, rounding up every single time introduces a small statistical bias over many roundings; to avoid this, the preceding digit is rounded to the nearest even digit instead.

**Step 2: Identify the digit to be dropped and the preceding digit**
Rounding 2.745 to 3 significant figures means dropping the final 5, and the digit immediately before it is 4.

**Step 3: Apply the even rule**
Since 4 is already even, it remains unchanged rather than being rounded up to 5.

**Final Answer**
The round-half-to-even convention keeps the digit at 4, giving 2.74.
Final answer: A) 2.74
questions.tip: Round-half-to-even only applies when the dropped part is exactly 5 with nothing further; if any non-zero digit follows the 5, always round up normally.

questions.text: A metre scale with a least count of 0.1 cm is used to measure a length, and a student records the result as 15.60 cm. Regarding significant figures, this recording is:
options: Incorrect as written; only 3 significant figures (15.6 cm) are justified, since writing 15.60 cm falsely implies a precision beyond the instrument's least count
Correct with 4 significant figures, since all four digits shown are valid
Correct with only 2 significant figures, since only whole centimetres are certain
Correct with 5 significant figures, since a trailing zero after a decimal point is always significant regardless of the instrument used
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how significant figures connect to measurement precision**
The number of significant figures in a reading should equal the number of digits that are certain (directly read off the scale) plus exactly one final estimated (uncertain) digit -- no more.

**Step 2: Apply this to the given least count**
With a least count of 0.1 cm, the scale can be read reliably to the tenths place, and the observer may estimate one digit beyond that; so the recorded length should stop at the tenths place, i.e. 15.6 cm, which has 3 significant figures.

**Step 3: See why 15.60 cm overstates the precision**
Writing an extra digit as 15.60 cm claims certainty down to the hundredths place (0.01 cm), a precision this particular instrument (least count 0.1 cm) simply cannot provide.

**Final Answer**
The correctly justified recording is 15.6 cm with 3 significant figures, not 15.60 cm.
Final answer: A) Incorrect as written; only 3 significant figures (15.6 cm) are justified, since writing 15.60 cm falsely implies a precision beyond the instrument's least count
questions.tip: The number of significant figures you report should always match what your instrument's least count can actually justify -- never write more digits than your measuring tool supports.
