questions.text: The relation connecting the current I in a conductor to the number density of free electrons n, the cross-sectional area A, the drift velocity v_{d} of the electrons, and the electronic charge e is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Picture the free electrons drifting**
Under an applied electric field, free electrons acquire a small average velocity v_{d} (the drift velocity) added on top of their random thermal motion. In a time t, every electron within a distance v_{d}t of a cross-section will cross it.

**Step 2: Count the charge crossing the area**
The volume swept up in time t is A v_{d} t, and with n electrons per unit volume this contains n A v_{d} t electrons, each of charge e.
\[ q = (nAv_{d}t)\,e \]

**Step 3: Convert charge to current**
Current is charge per unit time, so dividing by t gives the microscopic form of current.
\[ I = \dfrac{q}{t} = nAv_{d}e \]

**Final Answer**
This equation is the bridge between the microscopic motion of electrons and the macroscopic current we measure.
Final answer: A) I = nAv_{d}e
questions.tip: Memorise I = nAv_{d}e; it is the starting point for almost every drift-velocity numerical.

questions.text: Current density J at a point inside a current-carrying conductor is best described as
options: The total current in the conductor irrespective of area
The current per unit cross-sectional area, a vector along the direction of current flow
The current per unit volume of the conductor
The current per unit length of the conductor
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall why a local quantity is needed**
Current I is a property of the whole conductor, but the way charge flow is distributed can vary from point to point (especially in non-uniform conductors), so a local, point-based quantity is more useful for analysis.

**Step 2: Define current density**
Current density J is defined as the current per unit area held perpendicular to the flow, and it points in the direction conventional current flows at that point: \( \vec{J} = nq\vec{v_{d}} \).

**Step 3: Connect to total current**
Integrating J over any full cross-section recovers the total current, \( I = \int \vec{J}\cdot d\vec{A} \), confirming J is the area-density version of current.

**Final Answer**
Current density is a vector giving current per unit area in the direction of current flow.
Final answer: B) The current per unit cross-sectional area, a vector along the direction of current flow
questions.tip: Do not confuse current (scalar, whole conductor) with current density (vector, per unit area, local).

questions.text: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2} carries a current of 1.6 A. If the free electron density in copper is n = 8.5\times10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3} and e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}, the drift velocity of electrons in the wire is closest to
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the microscopic current formula**
Since I = nAv_{d}e, the drift velocity can be isolated by rearranging this relation.
\[ v_{d} = \dfrac{I}{nAe} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
\[ v_{d} = \dfrac{1.6}{(8.5\times10^{28})(1\times10^{-6})(1.6\times10^{-19})} \]

**Step 3: Simplify the denominator and compute**
The denominator is \(8.5\times1.6\times10^{28-6-19} = 13.6\times10^{3}\), so
\[ v_{d} = \dfrac{1.6}{1.36\times10^{4}} \approx 1.18\times10^{-4}\,\text{m/s} \]
This extremely small value explains why electrons drift far slower than one might expect despite the current flowing rapidly.

**Final Answer**
The drift velocity works out to about 1.18\times10^{-4} m/s, a typical order of magnitude for metals.
Final answer: C) 1.18\times10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}
questions.tip: Always plug values into v_{d} = I/(nAe) directly; keep powers of ten separate to avoid arithmetic slips.

questions.text: Although the drift velocity of electrons in a metallic conductor is only of the order of 10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}, an electric bulb connected to a distant switch glows almost the instant the switch is closed. This is because
options: The drift velocity of electrons is actually much higher than 10^{-4}\,\text{m/s} in practice
The electrons nearest to the bulb reach it almost instantaneously while distant electrons take longer
Current flows due to protons moving through the wire, which are much faster than electrons
The electric field that drives the electrons is established throughout the circuit almost instantaneously, close to the speed of light
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Separate two different speeds in the circuit**
There are two distinct things happening: individual electrons physically drifting (slow, ~10^{-4} m/s) and the electric field configuration that pushes every electron in the wire (fast).

**Step 2: Understand how the field propagates**
When the switch closes, the electromagnetic disturbance that establishes the electric field along the wire travels at a speed close to the speed of light, not at the drift speed.

**Step 3: See why the bulb glows instantly**
Because the field appears almost everywhere in the circuit almost simultaneously, all free electrons throughout the wire (including those already inside the bulb's filament) begin drifting together almost immediately, even though each individual electron moves slowly.

**Final Answer**
It is the near-instantaneous setup of the electric field, not the slow drift of individual electrons, that makes the bulb glow immediately.
Final answer: D) The electric field that drives the electrons is established throughout the circuit almost instantaneously, close to the speed of light
questions.tip: A classic NCERT conceptual trap: never confuse the slow drift speed with the fast speed at which the field (and hence the 'signal') propagates.

questions.text: A copper wire of diameter 1.6 mm carries a current of 2 A. The current density in the wire is closest to
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the cross-sectional area**
The radius is half the diameter, r = 0.8\,\text{mm} = 0.8\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}, so
\[ A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (0.8\times10^{-3})^{2} \approx 2.01\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2} \]

**Step 2: Apply the definition of current density**
Current density is current divided by the area it flows through.
\[ J = \dfrac{I}{A} \]

**Step 3: Substitute and compute**
\[ J = \dfrac{2}{2.01\times10^{-6}} \approx 9.9\times10^{5}\,\text{A/m}^{2} \]

**Final Answer**
The current density in the wire is about 9.9\times10^{5} A/m^{2}.
Final answer: A) 9.9\times10^{5}\,\text{A/m}^{2}
questions.tip: Always convert diameter to radius before squaring for area; a common slip is using diameter directly in \pi r^2.

questions.text: In a metal, the free-electron number density is n = 8.5\times10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3} and the relaxation time is \tau = 2.5\times10^{-14}\,\text{s}. Taking the electron mass m_{e} = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg} and e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}, the resistivity of the metal, using \rho = \dfrac{m_{e}}{n e^{2}\tau}, is closest to
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall where this formula comes from**
Combining v_{d} = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m_{e}} with J = nev_{d} and J = \sigma E gives conductivity \sigma = \dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m_{e}}, so resistivity is its reciprocal.
\[ \rho = \dfrac{m_{e}}{ne^{2}\tau} \]

**Step 2: Compute the denominator**
\[ ne^{2}\tau = (8.5\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})^{2}(2.5\times10^{-14}) \]
\[ = (8.5\times10^{28})(2.56\times10^{-38})(2.5\times10^{-14}) \approx 5.44\times10^{-23} \]

**Step 3: Divide to get resistivity**
\[ \rho = \dfrac{9.1\times10^{-31}}{5.44\times10^{-23}} \approx 1.67\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m} \]
This value matches the known resistivity of copper closely, confirming the microscopic model is consistent with real conductors.

**Final Answer**
The resistivity works out to about 1.67\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m}.
Final answer: B) 1.67\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m}
questions.tip: Keep track of powers of ten separately in \rho = m_e/(ne^2\tau); squaring e first (giving 10^{-38}) is where most mistakes happen.

questions.text: A wire of non-uniform cross-section has area A at point P and area 3A at point Q, and carries a steady current I. If the drift velocity at P is v_{P}, the drift velocity at Q is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recognise what stays constant**
Since the wire carries a steady current, I must be the same at every cross-section (charge cannot pile up anywhere in steady state), and the material (hence n) is the same throughout.

**Step 2: Write the drift velocity at each section**
From I = nAv_{d}e, the drift velocity satisfies \( v_{d} = \dfrac{I}{nAe} \), so v_{d} is inversely proportional to the local area A when I, n, e are fixed.

**Step 3: Compare the two sections**
\[ \dfrac{v_{Q}}{v_{P}} = \dfrac{A_{P}}{A_{Q}} = \dfrac{A}{3A} = \dfrac{1}{3} \]
So the drift velocity is three times smaller where the area is three times larger.

**Final Answer**
At the wider section Q, electrons need to drift more slowly to carry the same current.
Final answer: C) v_{P}/3
questions.tip: For a non-uniform wire with the same current everywhere, v_{d} \propto 1/A -- use this ratio shortcut instead of recomputing v_d from scratch at each point.

questions.text: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across it, provided that
options: the current flowing is very small
the resistance of the conductor varies with current
the physical conditions of the conductor, such as temperature, remain constant
questions.answer:
**Step 1: State the law precisely**
Ohm's law says V \propto I for a given conductor, which can be written as V = IR where R is treated as a constant of that conductor.

**Step 2: Identify the hidden condition**
R itself depends on properties like the conductor's resistivity, which changes with temperature. So R can only be treated as a true constant if the conductor's temperature (and other physical conditions) does not change while V and I are varied.

**Step 3: Contrast with non-ohmic behaviour**
Devices where R changes significantly as current flows (like a heated filament) or that inherently show a non-linear V-I graph (like diodes) do not obey Ohm's law even though V=IR can always be used to define an instantaneous resistance.

**Final Answer**
Ohm's law strictly holds only when the conductor's physical conditions, especially temperature, are kept constant.
Final answer: D) the physical conditions of the conductor, such as temperature, remain constant
questions.tip: Ohm's law is not a universal law of nature -- it is a property some materials (ohmic conductors) show under constant physical conditions.

questions.text: Which of the following is a non-ohmic device, i.e., does NOT obey Ohm's law?
options: A metallic wire at constant temperature
A carbon resistor at room temperature
A copper wire used in a torch circuit
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the test for ohmic behaviour**
A device obeys Ohm's law only if its V-I graph is a straight line through the origin, meaning V/I stays constant regardless of the applied voltage.

**Step 2: Examine each option's V-I behaviour**
Metallic wires, standard carbon resistors, and copper wires at constant temperature all show a linear V-I relationship over normal operating ranges, so they are ohmic.

**Step 3: Identify the exception**
A p-n junction diode conducts very differently in forward and reverse bias and shows a strongly non-linear (exponential-like) V-I curve, so V/I is far from constant.

**Final Answer**
The p-n junction diode is the classic example of a non-ohmic device taught alongside Ohm's law.
Final answer: A) A p-n junction diode
questions.tip: Diodes, transistors, and electrolytes with back EMF are the standard textbook examples of non-ohmic devices -- learn to recognise them by name.

questions.text: The V-I graph of a conductor is a straight line through the origin. If a potential difference of 6 V produces a current of 1.5 A, the resistance of the conductor is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall what a straight V-I line through the origin means**
Since V is directly proportional to I, the ratio V/I is a fixed number for every point on the line, and that constant ratio is exactly the resistance R.

**Step 2: Apply Ohm's law**
\[ R = \dfrac{V}{I} \]

**Step 3: Substitute the given values**
\[ R = \dfrac{6}{1.5} = 4\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The resistance of the conductor is 4 ohms.
Final answer: B) 4\,\Omega
questions.tip: On a V (y-axis) vs I (x-axis) graph, the slope directly gives resistance; on an I vs V graph, the slope gives 1/R instead.

questions.text: On a graph with potential difference V on the y-axis and current I on the x-axis, the straight line for conductor A is steeper than the straight line for conductor B. This means
options: Resistance of A is less than that of B
Resistance of A and B are equal
Resistance of A is greater than that of B
A is non-ohmic while B is ohmic
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall what the slope of a V-I graph represents**
Since V = IR, plotting V against I gives a straight line whose slope equals R for an ohmic conductor.

**Step 2: Compare slopes**
A steeper line means that a small increase in current produces a larger increase in voltage, which happens only when the conductor offers more opposition to current flow.

**Step 3: Conclude about resistance**
Since slope = R, a steeper V-I line for A directly implies R_{A} > R_{B}.

**Final Answer**
Because line A rises more steeply, its resistance must be greater than that of B.
Final answer: C) Resistance of A is greater than that of B
questions.tip: Whenever comparing two V-I graphs, translate 'steeper slope' directly into 'higher resistance' when V is on the y-axis.

questions.text: For a resistor, a graph is plotted with current I (in A) on the y-axis and voltage V (in V) on the x-axis. The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope 0.2\,\text{A/V}. The resistance of the resistor is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write Ohm's law with I as the dependent variable**
Rearranging V = IR gives \( I = \dfrac{1}{R}V \), so on an I-vs-V graph the slope equals \( \dfrac{1}{R} \), not R itself.

**Step 2: Use the given slope**
\[ \text{slope} = \dfrac{1}{R} = 0.2\,\text{A/V} \]

**Step 3: Solve for R**
\[ R = \dfrac{1}{0.2} = 5\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
Inverting the slope of the I-V graph gives a resistance of 5 ohms.
Final answer: D) 5\,\Omega
questions.tip: Watch which variable is on which axis -- an I-vs-V graph's slope is 1/R, the reverse of a V-vs-I graph's slope.

questions.text: The filament of a bulb has a resistance of 20\,\Omega at room temperature. When operated at its rated voltage of 220 V, it draws a current of 0.5 A. If the resistance increases linearly with temperature with temperature coefficient \alpha = 4.5\times10^{-3}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}, the rise in filament temperature above room temperature is approximately
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the operating resistance**
At the rated condition, Ohm's law gives the resistance while glowing.
\[ R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220}{0.5} = 440\,\Omega \]

**Step 2: Use the linear temperature-dependence relation**
A non-ohmic filament still satisfies R = R_{0}(1+\alpha\Delta T) locally, connecting resistance change to temperature rise.
\[ R = R_{0}(1+\alpha\Delta T) \]

**Step 3: Solve for \Delta T**
\[ \Delta T = \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{R_{0}}-1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{\dfrac{440}{20}-1}{4.5\times10^{-3}} = \dfrac{21}{0.0045} \approx 4667^{\circ}\text{C} \]
This large temperature rise (filament glowing white-hot) is exactly why the filament's V-I curve is far from a straight line.

**Final Answer**
The filament heats up by roughly 4667 degrees Celsius above room temperature when lit.
Final answer: A) 4667^{\circ}\text{C}
questions.tip: For filament-lamp problems, first find R at rated conditions from V and I, then use R = R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T) to link it to temperature.

questions.text: A student records the following V-I data for a conducting element: (V = 2 V, I = 1 A), (V = 4 V, I = 2.5 A), (V = 6 V, I = 4.5 A). Based on this data, the element
options: does not obey Ohm's law, since V/I is not constant
obeys Ohm's law only above 4 V
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the test for Ohm's law**
A conductor obeys Ohm's law only if the ratio V/I is the same at every data point, i.e., the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin.

**Step 2: Compute V/I for each pair**
\[ \dfrac{2}{1}=2\,\Omega,\quad \dfrac{4}{2.5}=1.6\,\Omega,\quad \dfrac{6}{4.5}\approx1.33\,\Omega \]

**Step 3: Interpret the trend**
The ratio V/I keeps decreasing as V increases, meaning the element's effective resistance is falling with increasing voltage -- this is inconsistent with a constant-resistance ohmic conductor.

**Final Answer**
Since V/I is not constant across the data, the element does not obey Ohm's law.
Final answer: B) does not obey Ohm's law, since V/I is not constant
questions.tip: When given a data table instead of a graph, always compute V/I at each point and check whether it stays constant before concluding a device is ohmic.

questions.text: The resistivity of a conducting wire, at a fixed temperature, depends upon
options: the cross-sectional area of the wire
the material of the wire only
both the length and the cross-sectional area of the wire
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Distinguish resistance from resistivity**
Resistance R depends on the geometry (length and area) as well as the material, but resistivity \rho is defined precisely to strip away the geometric dependence.

**Step 2: Recall the defining relation**
\[ R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \rho = \dfrac{RA}{L} \]
Here \rho is an intrinsic property that characterises how strongly a given material opposes current flow, independent of the sample's shape.

**Step 3: Conclude what resistivity depends on**
At a fixed temperature, \rho is the same for all wires of a given material regardless of their length or thickness; it changes only if the material itself changes (or its temperature changes).

**Final Answer**
Resistivity is purely a material property at a given temperature, unlike resistance which also depends on dimensions.
Final answer: C) the material of the wire only
questions.tip: Resistance changes with geometry; resistivity does not -- this distinction is a favourite conceptual MCQ trap.

questions.text: If the length of a wire of uniform cross-section is doubled while its material and cross-sectional area remain unchanged, its resistance
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the resistance formula**
Resistance depends on length, area, and resistivity through
\[ R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A} \]

**Step 2: Identify what changes**
Here \rho (material) and A stay fixed, while L is doubled to 2L.

**Step 3: Compute the new resistance**
\[ R' = \rho \dfrac{2L}{A} = 2\left(\rho \dfrac{L}{A}\right) = 2R \]

**Final Answer**
Doubling the length while keeping area and material fixed simply doubles the resistance.
Final answer: D) becomes double
questions.tip: R is directly proportional to length and inversely proportional to area -- change one factor at a time to track the effect.

questions.text: As temperature increases, the resistance of a pure metallic conductor generally
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Think about what resistance depends on microscopically**
Resistance arises from collisions between free electrons and the vibrating lattice ions; more frequent or more violent collisions mean shorter relaxation time \tau and hence higher resistance.

**Step 2: Consider the effect of heating a metal**
As temperature rises, the ions of the metallic lattice vibrate with larger amplitude, increasing the frequency of electron-ion collisions and reducing \tau, while the number density n of free electrons stays essentially constant.

**Step 3: Relate this to resistivity**
Since \( \rho = \dfrac{m_{e}}{ne^{2}\tau} \), a decrease in \tau with roughly constant n directly increases \rho, and hence R.

**Final Answer**
For pure metals, increased lattice vibration at higher temperature raises resistance.
Final answer: A) increases
questions.tip: Metals: resistance rises with temperature (positive \alpha). Semiconductors and insulators typically show the opposite trend.

questions.text: A wire has resistivity 1.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m}, length 2 m, and cross-sectional area 1\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2}. Its resistance is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write the resistance formula**
\[ R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
\[ R = (1.7\times10^{-8}) \times \dfrac{2}{1\times10^{-6}} \]

**Step 3: Simplify**
\[ R = (1.7\times10^{-8})(2\times10^{6}) = 3.4\times10^{-2}\,\Omega = 0.034\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The wire's resistance comes out to 0.034 ohms.
Final answer: B) 0.034\,\Omega
questions.tip: Keep resistivity values in scientific notation throughout to avoid decimal errors when computing R = \rho L/A.

questions.text: A wire of resistance R is stretched uniformly so that its length becomes twice the original length, with its volume remaining unchanged. The new resistance is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Use volume conservation to find the new area**
Since volume V = AL stays fixed while L doubles to 2L, the new area must satisfy A'(2L) = AL, giving \( A' = A/2 \).

**Step 2: Write the new resistance in terms of the new dimensions**
\[ R' = \rho \dfrac{L'}{A'} = \rho \dfrac{2L}{A/2} = 4\rho\dfrac{L}{A} \]

**Step 3: Compare with the original resistance**
Since \( R = \rho L/A \), this shows
\[ R' = 4R \]
Physically, resistance grows as the square of the stretch factor because both the increased length and the thinned cross-section work in the same direction.

**Final Answer**
Stretching a wire to twice its length at constant volume quadruples its resistance.
Final answer: C) 4R
questions.tip: For 'stretched wire, volume constant' problems, remember R \propto L^{2} (since R' /R = (L'/L)^2) -- a very common shortcut.

questions.text: A copper coil has resistance 20\,\Omega at 20^{\circ}\text{C}. If the temperature coefficient of resistance of copper is 4\times10^{-3}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}, its resistance at 70^{\circ}\text{C} is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the temperature change**
\[ \Delta T = 70^{\circ}\text{C} - 20^{\circ}\text{C} = 50^{\circ}\text{C} \]

**Step 2: Apply the linear temperature-resistance relation**
\[ R_{T} = R_{0}(1+\alpha\Delta T) \]

**Step 3: Substitute and compute**
\[ R_{T} = 20\left(1 + (4\times10^{-3})(50)\right) = 20(1+0.2) = 20\times1.2 = 24\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The coil's resistance rises to 24 ohms at the higher temperature.
Final answer: D) 24\,\Omega
questions.tip: In R_t = R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T), always use \Delta T (temperature change), not the final temperature itself.

questions.text: Unlike metals, the resistance of a pure semiconductor decreases as its temperature increases. This is mainly because
options: the number density of charge carriers increases rapidly with temperature, outweighing the increase in collisions
the relaxation time of electrons increases sharply with temperature
the charge on each electron decreases at higher temperature
semiconductors have no free electrons at low temperature and hence infinite resistance
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall what resistivity depends on**
\[ \rho = \dfrac{m_{e}}{ne^{2}\tau} \]
Both n (carrier density) and \tau (relaxation time) can change with temperature, and their combined effect determines whether \rho rises or falls.

**Step 2: Consider the semiconductor case specifically**
In a semiconductor, raising the temperature breaks more covalent bonds, generating a large number of additional free electrons and holes -- n increases very steeply (often exponentially) with temperature.

**Step 3: Compare the competing effects**
Although \tau does decrease somewhat due to increased lattice vibrations (just as in metals), the explosive rise in n dominates completely, causing \rho -- and hence resistance -- to fall overall.

**Final Answer**
The sharp rise in charge-carrier density with temperature is what makes semiconductor resistance decrease, unlike in metals.
Final answer: A) the number density of charge carriers increases rapidly with temperature, outweighing the increase in collisions
questions.tip: For semiconductors, focus on the change in carrier density n; for metals, focus on the change in relaxation time \tau.

questions.text: The resistance of a platinum wire is 5\,\Omega at 0^{\circ}\text{C} and 6.8\,\Omega at 100^{\circ}\text{C}. Using R_{t} = R_{0}(1+\alpha t), the temperature coefficient of resistance of platinum is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the temperature-resistance relation**
\[ R_{t} = R_{0}(1+\alpha t) \]

**Step 2: Substitute the given data**
\[ 6.8 = 5\left(1+\alpha(100)\right) \]

**Step 3: Solve for \alpha**
\[ \dfrac{6.8}{5} = 1+100\alpha \quad\Rightarrow\quad 1.36-1 = 100\alpha \quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha = \dfrac{0.36}{100} = 3.6\times10^{-3}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1} \]

**Final Answer**
The temperature coefficient of resistance of the platinum wire is 3.6\times10^{-3} per degree Celsius.
Final answer: B) 3.6\times10^{-3}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}
questions.tip: This is the standard method used in resistance thermometers to measure temperature -- rearrange R_t = R_0(1+\alpha t) to solve for whichever quantity is unknown.

questions.text: Two wires A and B made of the same material have equal resistance. If the length of A is twice the length of B, the ratio of their cross-sectional areas A_{A} : A_{B} is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write the resistance of each wire**
Same material means the same resistivity \rho for both wires.
\[ R_{A} = \rho\dfrac{L_{A}}{A_{A}}, \qquad R_{B} = \rho\dfrac{L_{B}}{A_{B}} \]

**Step 2: Use the condition R_{A} = R_{B}**
\[ \dfrac{L_{A}}{A_{A}} = \dfrac{L_{B}}{A_{B}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{A_{A}}{A_{B}} = \dfrac{L_{A}}{L_{B}} \]

**Step 3: Substitute the length ratio**
Since L_{A} = 2L_{B},
\[ \dfrac{A_{A}}{A_{B}} = \dfrac{2L_{B}}{L_{B}} = 2 \]

**Final Answer**
For equal resistance with double the length, the longer wire must also have double the cross-sectional area.
Final answer: C) 2 : 1
questions.tip: When resistance and material are both fixed, R \propto L/A becomes constant, so A must scale exactly with L.

questions.text: The electrical power P dissipated in a resistor of resistance R, carrying current I, with potential difference V across it, can correctly be expressed as
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Start from the basic definition of electrical power**
Power delivered to a circuit element is the rate at which it does work moving charge through a potential difference, giving the most fundamental form:
\[ P = VI \]

**Step 2: Substitute Ohm's law to get alternate forms**
Using V = IR, replace V in P = VI to get \( P = I^{2}R \), or replace I with V/R to get \( P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R} \).

**Step 3: Recognise all three forms are equivalent**
All three expressions describe the same physical power, just written using different pairs of the three quantities V, I, R -- useful depending on which two are known in a problem.

**Final Answer**
All three power formulas are valid and interchangeable via Ohm's law.
Final answer: D) P = VI = I^{2}R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}
questions.tip: Choose the power formula that uses the quantities already given in the problem to avoid extra calculation steps.

questions.text: The heat produced in a resistor of resistance R when a current I flows through it for a time t, according to Joule's law of heating, is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the source of Joule heating**
As current flows through a resistor, electrons repeatedly collide with the lattice, transferring their kinetic energy as heat -- this is dissipated at the same rate as electrical power is delivered.

**Step 2: Connect power to heat over time**
Since power P is energy per unit time, the total heat generated in time t equals power multiplied by time.
\[ H = Pt \]

**Step 3: Substitute the power formula in terms of I and R**
Using \( P = I^{2}R \),
\[ H = I^{2}Rt \]

**Final Answer**
Joule's law of heating gives the heat dissipated as H = I^{2}Rt.
Final answer: A) H = I^{2}Rt
questions.tip: Joule heating always uses I^{2}Rt, not IRt -- resistive heating depends on the square of the current.

questions.text: An electric bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. The resistance of its filament at operating temperature, and the current drawn from the supply, are respectively
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Use the rated power and voltage to find resistance**
The rated values mean that at V = 220 V, the bulb consumes P = 100 W, so
\[ R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{100} = \dfrac{48400}{100} = 484\,\Omega \]

**Step 2: Find the current from the power and voltage**
\[ I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{100}{220} \approx 0.45\,\text{A} \]

**Step 3: Cross-check using Ohm's law**
\[ I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{220}{484} \approx 0.45\,\text{A} \]
Both methods agree, confirming the values.

**Final Answer**
The filament resistance is 484 ohms and it draws about 0.45 A at rated operation.
Final answer: B) 484\,\Omega \text{ and } 0.45\,\text{A}
questions.tip: For rated-power bulb problems, use R = V^2/P to get resistance directly from the nameplate values.

questions.text: Two bulbs rated 100 W-220 V and 60 W-220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which bulb glows brighter, and why?
options: The 100 W bulb glows brighter because it is rated for higher power
Both bulbs glow equally bright since they carry the same current
The 60 W bulb glows brighter because it has higher resistance and dissipates more power for the same series current
The 60 W bulb does not glow at all when connected in series
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the resistance of each bulb from its rating**
\[ R_{100} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{100} = 484\,\Omega, \qquad R_{60} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{60} \approx 806.7\,\Omega \]
The lower-wattage bulb actually has the higher resistance.

**Step 2: Recognise the series-circuit constraint**
In series, both bulbs carry exactly the same current I, since charge cannot accumulate at the junction between them.

**Step 3: Compare power dissipated using P = I^{2}R**
Since I is common, power dissipated is directly proportional to resistance, so the bulb with larger R dissipates more power and glows brighter -- this is the 60 W bulb.

**Final Answer**
In series, the lower-wattage (higher-resistance) bulb glows brighter, opposite to what happens in parallel.
Final answer: C) The 60 W bulb glows brighter because it has higher resistance and dissipates more power for the same series current
questions.tip: Series circuits: same current flows, so higher-resistance (lower-rated) bulb glows brighter. Parallel circuits: same voltage, so higher-rated bulb glows brighter -- the two situations are reversed.

questions.text: A 2000 W electric heater is used for 3 hours daily. If the cost of electricity is Rs 6 per unit (kWh), the cost of running the heater for 30 days is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Convert power to kilowatts**
\[ P = 2000\,\text{W} = 2\,\text{kW} \]

**Step 2: Compute total energy consumed over 30 days**
Energy in kWh equals power (kW) times total hours of use.
\[ E = 2\,\text{kW} \times 3\,\text{h/day} \times 30\,\text{days} = 180\,\text{kWh} \]

**Step 3: Multiply by the cost per unit**
\[ \text{Cost} = 180 \times 6 = \text{Rs } 1080 \]

**Final Answer**
Running the heater for 3 hours a day over 30 days costs Rs 1080.
Final answer: D) \text{Rs } 1080
questions.tip: For electricity-bill problems, always convert power to kW first so that energy comes out directly in kWh (the 'unit' of billing).

questions.text: A current of 5 A flows through a resistor of 10\,\Omega for 2 minutes. The heat generated in the resistor is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Convert time to seconds**
\[ t = 2\,\text{min} = 120\,\text{s} \]

**Step 2: Apply Joule's law of heating**
\[ H = I^{2}Rt \]

**Step 3: Substitute the values**
\[ H = (5)^{2}(10)(120) = 25\times10\times120 = 30000\,\text{J} = 3\times10^{4}\,\text{J} \]

**Final Answer**
The resistor generates 3\times10^{4} joules of heat.
Final answer: D) 3\times10^{4}\,\text{J}
questions.tip: Always convert time to seconds before using H = I^2Rt, since resistance and current are in SI units.

questions.text: A cell of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2\,\Omega is connected to a variable external resistance R. The value of R for which the power delivered to R is maximum, and that maximum power, are
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write the power delivered to R**
The current in the loop is \( I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R+r} \), so the power delivered to R is
\[ P = I^{2}R = \dfrac{\varepsilon^{2}R}{(R+r)^{2}} \]

**Step 2: Recall the maximum power transfer condition**
Maximising P with respect to R (by calculus, or by recognising this is a standard result) shows P is maximum when the external resistance equals the internal resistance, R = r.
\[ R = r = 2\,\Omega \]

**Step 3: Compute the maximum power**
At R = r, the current is \( I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2r} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3\,\text{A} \), so
\[ P_{max} = I^{2}R = (3)^{2}(2) = 18\,\text{W} \]
Alternatively, \( P_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4r} = \dfrac{144}{8} = 18\,\text{W} \), confirming the result.

**Final Answer**
Maximum power transfer occurs at R = 2 ohms, delivering 18 W to the external resistor.
Final answer: B) R = 2\,\Omega,\ P_{max} = 18\,\text{W}
questions.tip: Memorise the maximum power transfer result directly: R = r gives P_{max} = \varepsilon^{2}/(4r) -- it saves time versus differentiating in the exam.

questions.text: Two identical resistors, each of resistance R, are first connected in series and then in parallel across the same supply voltage V. The ratio of the heat generated per second in the parallel combination to that in the series combination is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the equivalent resistance in each case**
In series, R_{s} = R + R = 2R. In parallel, \( \dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{R}+\dfrac{1}{R} \), giving \( R_{p} = R/2 \).

**Step 2: Write the power dissipated in each case using P = V^{2}/R_{eq}**
Since the same voltage V is applied across the whole combination in both cases,
\[ P_{s} = \dfrac{V^{2}}{2R}, \qquad P_{p} = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R/2} = \dfrac{2V^{2}}{R} \]

**Step 3: Take the ratio**
\[ \dfrac{P_{p}}{P_{s}} = \dfrac{2V^{2}/R}{V^{2}/2R} = \dfrac{2V^{2}}{R}\times\dfrac{2R}{V^{2}} = 4 \]

**Final Answer**
The parallel combination dissipates heat four times faster than the series combination for the same supply voltage.
Final answer: C) 4 : 1
questions.tip: For identical resistors across the same voltage, parallel combination always dissipates more power than series -- here exactly R_p/R_s = 1/4 gives a power ratio of 4.

questions.text: Kirchhoff's current law (the junction rule) states that at any junction in an electrical circuit
options: the sum of all currents entering the junction exceeds the sum leaving it
the junction rule applies only to circuits containing a single loop
current entering a junction is always equal to the EMF of the circuit
the algebraic sum of currents meeting at the junction is zero
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the underlying physical principle**
Charge cannot be created, destroyed, or accumulated indefinitely at a point in a steady-state circuit, so whatever charge flows into a junction per second must flow out per second.

**Step 2: State the rule in terms of currents**
Taking currents entering a junction as positive and currents leaving as negative (or vice versa), their algebraic sum at any instant must equal zero.
\[ \sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out} \quad\text{i.e.,}\quad \sum I = 0 \]

**Step 3: Note its generality**
This rule applies at every junction of any circuit, no matter how many loops or branches it has -- it is simply a statement of charge conservation.

**Final Answer**
Kirchhoff's current law is the algebraic-sum-zero statement of charge conservation at a junction.
Final answer: D) the algebraic sum of currents meeting at the junction is zero
questions.tip: KCL = charge conservation at a point; KVL = energy conservation around a loop -- keep these two rules and their justifications separate.

questions.text: Kirchhoff's voltage law (the loop rule) is fundamentally based on the principle of
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall what potential difference represents**
The electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge to bring a charge from a reference point to that point; it is a well-defined, path-independent quantity in an electrostatic-like circuit field.

**Step 2: Consider a charge taken around a closed loop**
If a charge is moved around any closed loop in the circuit and returns to its starting point, the net work done on it, and hence the net change in potential energy, must be zero, since potential is single-valued at each point.

**Step 3: Express this as the loop rule**
\[ \sum \Delta V = 0 \text{ around any closed loop} \]
This is exactly a statement that energy gained from EMF sources equals energy lost across resistors in one complete trip around the loop.

**Final Answer**
The loop rule is a direct consequence of energy conservation applied to charge moving around a closed circuit.
Final answer: A) conservation of energy
questions.tip: If asked why the loop rule works, always answer 'energy conservation / potential is a single-valued function of position'.

questions.text: While applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, if a resistor is traversed in the same direction as the assumed current flowing through it, the potential
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the physical reason for a potential drop across a resistor**
Current flows from higher to lower potential through a resistor (in the direction of conventional current), since the resistor dissipates energy as the charge passes through it.

**Step 2: Apply this to loop-traversal sign convention**
If you traverse the resistor in the same direction the current is flowing, you are moving from the higher-potential end to the lower-potential end, so the potential change you record is negative.

**Step 3: Write the magnitude of the change**
The magnitude of the drop equals the product of current and resistance by Ohm's law, so the signed change is
\[ \Delta V = -IR \]

**Final Answer**
Traversing a resistor along the current direction gives a potential drop of IR.
Final answer: B) drops by IR (the change is -IR)
questions.tip: Sign convention shortcut: moving along assumed current through a resistor -> -IR; moving against it -> +IR; through a cell from - to + terminal -> +EMF.

questions.text: In a single-loop circuit, a cell of EMF 10 V with negligible internal resistance drives current through two resistors of 3\,\Omega and 2\,\Omega connected in series. Using Kirchhoff's voltage law, the current in the circuit is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the loop rule around the single loop**
Going around the loop, the EMF gained equals the total IR drop across both resistors (traversed in the direction of current).
\[ \varepsilon = I R_{1} + I R_{2} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
\[ 10 = I(3) + I(2) = I(5) \]

**Step 3: Solve for the current**
\[ I = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
The current flowing around the single loop is 2 A.
Final answer: C) 2\,\text{A}
questions.tip: For a single-loop circuit with resistors purely in series, the loop rule just reduces to \varepsilon = I\sum R -- no need for simultaneous equations.

questions.text: At a junction in a circuit, currents of 3 A and 2 A flow into the junction, while a current I_{1} flows out along one branch and 1 A flows out along another. Using Kirchhoff's junction rule, I_{1} equals
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the junction rule**
Charge conservation requires the total current entering a junction to equal the total current leaving it.
\[ \sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out} \]

**Step 2: Write the currents in and out**
\[ 3 + 2 = I_{1} + 1 \]

**Step 3: Solve for I_{1}**
\[ 5 = I_{1} + 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad I_{1} = 4\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
The unknown outgoing current I_{1} must be 4 A to balance the junction.
Final answer: D) 4\,\text{A}
questions.tip: List all currents into a junction on one side and all currents out on the other, then simply equate the two sums.

questions.text: Two cells of EMF 6 V and 4 V (negligible internal resistance) are connected in series opposition in a loop containing a resistor of 2\,\Omega. The current in the circuit is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Understand 'series opposition'**
When two cells are connected so that they oppose each other, the net EMF driving current around the loop is the difference of the two EMFs, not their sum.

**Step 2: Find the net EMF**
\[ \varepsilon_{net} = 6 - 4 = 2\,\text{V} \]

**Step 3: Apply the loop rule to find current**
\[ \varepsilon_{net} = IR \quad\Rightarrow\quad I = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
The net driving EMF of 2 V pushes a current of 1 A through the 2-ohm resistor.
Final answer: A) 1\,\text{A}
questions.tip: For opposing cells, subtract the smaller EMF from the larger; for aiding cells connected the same way round, add them.

questions.text: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1\,\Omega is connected to an external resistor of 5\,\Omega. Using Kirchhoff's voltage law, the terminal voltage of the battery is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Apply the loop rule to find the current**
Going around the loop, the EMF equals the sum of the IR drops across the internal and external resistances.
\[ \varepsilon = I(R+r) \quad\Rightarrow\quad I = \dfrac{12}{5+1} = 2\,\text{A} \]

**Step 2: Recall the meaning of terminal voltage**
The terminal voltage is what a voltmeter would read across the battery's terminals -- it is the EMF minus the voltage dropped internally, since some energy is lost overcoming internal resistance.
\[ V = \varepsilon - Ir \]

**Step 3: Substitute and compute**
\[ V = 12 - (2)(1) = 10\,\text{V} \]
This matches the voltage across the external resistor: \( V = IR = (2)(5) = 10\,\text{V} \), confirming consistency.

**Final Answer**
The terminal voltage of the battery, once internal resistance is accounted for, is 10 V.
Final answer: B) 10\,\text{V}
questions.tip: Terminal voltage V = \varepsilon - Ir when discharging (delivering current), and V = \varepsilon + Ir when charging -- know both cases.

questions.text: Applying Kirchhoff's laws to a two-loop circuit yields the simultaneous equations \( 3I_{1}+2I_{2}=3 \) and \( 2I_{1}+3I_{2}=6 \), where I_{1} and I_{2} are the loop currents in amperes. The value of I_{2} is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up elimination**
Multiply the first equation by 3 and the second by 2 so that the I_{2} terms match, allowing elimination.
\[ 9I_{1}+6I_{2}=9 \qquad 4I_{1}+6I_{2}=12 \]

**Step 2: Subtract to eliminate I_{2}**
\[ (9I_{1}+6I_{2}) - (4I_{1}+6I_{2}) = 9-12 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 5I_{1} = -3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad I_{1} = -0.6\,\text{A} \]
The negative sign simply means this loop current actually flows opposite to the direction originally assumed -- a normal outcome in Kirchhoff's law problems.

**Step 3: Substitute back to find I_{2}**
\[ 3(-0.6) + 2I_{2} = 3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad -1.8 + 2I_{2} = 3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2I_{2} = 4.8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad I_{2} = 2.4\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
Solving the simultaneous Kirchhoff equations gives I_{2} = 2.4 A.
Final answer: C) 2.4\,\text{A}
questions.tip: A negative loop current from Kirchhoff's equations is not an error -- it means the actual current direction is opposite to the one you assumed.

questions.text: In a circuit, a single loop contains a battery of EMF 10 V (internal resistance 1\,\Omega) in series with resistors of 2\,\Omega and 3\,\Omega, and a second, opposing battery of EMF 4 V (internal resistance 1\,\Omega). Using Kirchhoff's voltage law, the current in the loop is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Find the net EMF driving the loop**
Since the second battery opposes the first, the effective EMF around the loop is their difference.
\[ \varepsilon_{net} = 10 - 4 = 6\,\text{V} \]

**Step 2: Add up all resistances in the single loop**
All elements are in series, so total resistance is the sum of both internal resistances and both external resistors.
\[ R_{total} = 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 7\,\Omega \]

**Step 3: Apply the loop rule**
\[ \varepsilon_{net} = IR_{total} \quad\Rightarrow\quad I = \dfrac{6}{7} \approx 0.86\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
The net EMF of 6 V drives a current of about 0.86 A around the loop against a total resistance of 7 ohms.
Final answer: D) \dfrac{6}{7}\,\text{A} \approx 0.86\,\text{A}
questions.tip: In a single series loop with opposing cells, always include every internal resistance in the total resistance sum, and use the net (difference) EMF.

questions.text: Three resistors of 2\,\Omega, 3\,\Omega, and 6\,\Omega are connected in parallel between the same two nodes A and B, and a total current of 11 A enters the combination at A. Since all three resistors share the same potential difference V, the current through the 2\,\Omega resistor is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Use the junction rule to relate the branch currents to V**
Since all three resistors are between the same two nodes, each has the same potential difference V, and by Kirchhoff's current law the total current entering equals the sum of the three branch currents.
\[ 11 = \dfrac{V}{2} + \dfrac{V}{3} + \dfrac{V}{6} \]

**Step 2: Combine the fractions and solve for V**
\[ \dfrac{V}{2}+\dfrac{V}{3}+\dfrac{V}{6} = V\left(\dfrac{3+2+1}{6}\right) = V \]
So \( 11 = V \), giving \( V = 11\,\text{V} \).

**Step 3: Find the current through the 2\,\Omega resistor**
\[ I_{2\Omega} = \dfrac{V}{2} = \dfrac{11}{2} = 5.5\,\text{A} \]

**Final Answer**
Applying the junction rule with the common voltage across parallel branches gives 5.5 A through the 2-ohm resistor.
Final answer: A) 5.5\,\text{A}
questions.tip: For resistors in parallel between the same two nodes, first find the common voltage V by summing V/R_i for each branch and equating to the total current, then use V to get any individual branch current.

questions.text: In a Wheatstone bridge with resistances P, Q, R, S in its four arms and a galvanometer connected across the bridge, the balance (null-deflection) condition is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the bridge condition**
The bridge is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which means the potential at the two junctions it connects must be equal.

**Step 2: Apply this to the two potential-divider arms**
With no galvanometer current, P and Q form one potential divider and R and S form the other, both fed by the same battery current paths, so equal potential at the middle nodes requires the same fractional voltage drop in each pair.

**Step 3: Write the resulting balance condition**
\[ \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S} \]
This is the standard Wheatstone bridge balance condition used to find an unknown resistance when the other three are known.

**Final Answer**
The bridge balances when the ratio of resistances in one pair of arms equals the ratio in the other pair.
Final answer: B) \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}
questions.tip: Memorise P/Q = R/S as the balance condition; it is the single most important formula for this topic.

questions.text: A meter bridge is a practical form of the Wheatstone bridge used to measure an unknown resistance. It works on the principle that at the balance (null) point
options: maximum current flows through the galvanometer
the unknown resistance equals the resistance of the meter bridge wire
no current flows through the galvanometer
the current in the two gaps is always equal to the current in the wire
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the underlying bridge structure**
A meter bridge replaces two arms of a Wheatstone bridge with a single uniform resistance wire, and the balance point (jockey position) divides this wire into two effective resistances.

**Step 2: Recall what 'balance' means for the galvanometer**
Just as in a standard Wheatstone bridge, balance is defined as the specific jockey position where the galvanometer shows zero deflection, meaning the two junctions it bridges are at equal potential.

**Step 3: Connect this to zero current**
Equal potential at both ends of the galvanometer branch means there is no potential difference to drive current through it, so the galvanometer current is exactly zero at balance.

**Final Answer**
The null point of a meter bridge is defined by zero current through the galvanometer.
Final answer: C) no current flows through the galvanometer
questions.tip: The meter bridge is literally a Wheatstone bridge with two arms replaced by segments of one wire -- all Wheatstone bridge reasoning applies directly.

questions.text: In a meter bridge experiment, the balance point is preferably obtained near the middle of the wire (around the 50 cm mark) because
options: the wire is thickest at the middle
the galvanometer is sensitive only at the midpoint
the resistance of the wire is zero at the midpoint
the percentage error in the measurement of length is minimum there, giving the most accurate result
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the meter bridge formula**
The unknown resistance is calculated from the balance length l using \( X = R\dfrac{100-l}{l} \) (or the equivalent ratio form), so any small error in reading l translates into an error in X.

**Step 2: Analyse how the error in l affects the result**
The sensitivity of the meter bridge (how much the balance point shifts for a small mismatch in resistances) is greatest when l is near 50 cm; near the two ends, a small absolute error in reading the jockey position causes a disproportionately large percentage error in X.

**Step 3: Conclude the experimental practice**
By choosing the known resistance R so that the balance point falls close to the middle of the wire, the fractional error in the measured unknown resistance is minimised.

**Final Answer**
Balance points near the middle of the wire give the most accurate value of the unknown resistance because the percentage error there is smallest.
Final answer: D) the percentage error in the measurement of length is minimum there, giving the most accurate result
questions.tip: A common lab-based conceptual question: always answer 'minimum percentage error near 50 cm', a key practical point for the meter bridge experiment.

questions.text: In a Wheatstone bridge, the resistances in the four arms are P = 4\,\Omega, Q = 8\,\Omega, R = 6\,\Omega, and the unknown resistance S. For the bridge to be balanced, the value of S is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write the balance condition**
\[ \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
\[ \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{6}{S} \]

**Step 3: Solve for S**
\[ S = \dfrac{6\times8}{4} = \dfrac{48}{4} = 12\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The unknown arm S must be 12 ohms to balance this bridge.
Final answer: D) 12\,\Omega
questions.tip: Cross-multiply the balance ratio directly: S = RQ/P -- rearrange P/Q = R/S carefully so the unknown ends up correctly placed.

questions.text: In a meter bridge experiment, a resistance of 10\,\Omega is placed in the left gap and an unknown resistance X in the right gap. The null point is obtained at 40 cm from the left end. The value of X is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the meter bridge balance condition**
The wire is split at the null point into a length l (left, corresponding to the known resistance R) and 100-l (right, corresponding to X), and the balance condition mirrors the Wheatstone bridge ratio.
\[ \dfrac{R}{X} = \dfrac{l}{100-l} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
\[ \dfrac{10}{X} = \dfrac{40}{60} \]

**Step 3: Solve for X**
\[ X = 10\times\dfrac{60}{40} = 15\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The unknown resistance in the right gap is 15 ohms.
Final answer: B) 15\,\Omega
questions.tip: In a meter bridge, resistance ratio equals wire-length ratio on the same side: R/X = l/(100-l) -- match each resistance to the length on its own side of the jockey.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, an unknown resistance X is connected in the left gap and a standard resistance of 15\,\Omega in the right gap. The balance point is found at 60 cm from the left end. The unknown resistance X is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the balance condition with X on the left**
Since X is in the left gap (corresponding to the length l from the left end) and 15\,\Omega is in the right gap (corresponding to 100-l),
\[ \dfrac{X}{15} = \dfrac{l}{100-l} \]

**Step 2: Substitute the balance length**
\[ \dfrac{X}{15} = \dfrac{60}{40} = 1.5 \]

**Step 3: Solve for X**
\[ X = 15 \times 1.5 = 22.5\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The unknown resistance in the left gap is 22.5 ohms.
Final answer: C) 22.5\,\Omega
questions.tip: Always match the correct resistance to the correct side of the balance point -- swapping gaps flips which resistance goes with l and which with (100-l).

questions.text: In a meter bridge, when the resistances placed in the two gaps are interchanged, the balance point shifts from 40 cm to 60 cm (both measured from the same end). This behaviour is expected because
options: the bridge becomes permanently unbalanced after interchanging
the resistance of the bridge wire itself changes when the gaps are interchanged
the resistance of the galvanometer changes when the gaps are interchanged
interchanging P and Q gives a balance length of (100-l) from the same end, a check used to eliminate end corrections
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Write the balance condition before interchanging**
If the balance is at length l with resistances R (left) and X (right), \( \dfrac{R}{X} = \dfrac{l}{100-l} \).

**Step 2: Write the balance condition after interchanging**
After swapping so X is on the left and R is on the right, the roles of l and 100-l swap in the formula, so the new balance length l' satisfies \( \dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l'}{100-l'} \), which is the reciprocal of the original ratio.

**Step 3: Show this predicts l' = 100 - l**
Since the new ratio is the reciprocal of the old one, solving gives \( l' = 100 - l \); here 100 - 40 = 60, matching the observed shift exactly.

**Final Answer**
This interchange technique is a standard check in the meter bridge experiment used to eliminate end corrections (resistance of connecting wires and contacts).
Final answer: D) interchanging P and Q gives a balance length of (100-l) from the same end, a check used to eliminate end corrections
questions.tip: The interchange-of-resistances trick (checking l' = 100 - l) is a standard meter-bridge lab technique used to correct for end resistances -- remember it as a practical, not just theoretical, tool.

questions.text: In a Post Office Box (a Wheatstone-bridge-based resistance box), the ratio arms are set as P = 100\,\Omega and Q = 10\,\Omega, and the resistance arm is varied for balance to R = 63.5\,\Omega. Using the balance condition X = \dfrac{Q}{P}R for the unknown resistance X, its value is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall that a Post Office Box is just a compact Wheatstone bridge**
Its ratio arms P and Q set a scaling factor, while the resistance arm R is adjusted in known steps until the galvanometer shows null deflection.

**Step 2: Apply the balance condition in the form given**
\[ X = \dfrac{Q}{P}R \]

**Step 3: Substitute the given values**
\[ X = \dfrac{10}{100}\times63.5 = 0.1\times63.5 = 6.35\,\Omega \]

**Final Answer**
The unknown resistance measured by the Post Office Box is 6.35 ohms.
Final answer: A) 6.35\,\Omega
questions.tip: In a Post Office Box, the ratio arms (P, Q) act as a multiplier on the resistance arm R -- choosing P/Q appropriately lets you measure both very small and very large unknown resistances precisely.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, resistances of 6\,\Omega and 10\,\Omega are placed in the left and right gaps respectively. Neglecting end corrections, the balance point measured from the left end is
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the balance condition**
With 6\,\Omega on the left (corresponding to length l) and 10\,\Omega on the right (corresponding to 100-l),
\[ \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{l}{100-l} \]

**Step 2: Cross-multiply**
\[ 6(100-l) = 10l \quad\Rightarrow\quad 600 - 6l = 10l \]

**Step 3: Solve for l**
\[ 600 = 16l \quad\Rightarrow\quad l = \dfrac{600}{16} = 37.5\,\text{cm} \]

**Final Answer**
The balance point occurs at 37.5 cm from the left end, where the 6-ohm resistor is connected.
Final answer: B) 37.5\,\text{cm}
questions.tip: Since the smaller resistance is on the left, expect the balance point to fall before the 50 cm mark -- use this as a quick sanity check on your algebra.
